{"version":1,"content":"

WHAT EACH NODE DOES

The colour of a node tells you what kind of node it is. Nothing here needs changing except the blue ones.

 Models to download

Orange. Each one needs a file from the list in the note above.

  • Load Diffusion Model (Ming Image 0.1 Design) - The image model itself, 6B, from inclusionAI (Ant Group). It is made for design: posters, flyers, ads, UI screens, infographics, anything with text.
  • Load CLIP (Ling mini 2.0) - Reads your prompt and looks at your picture.
  • Load VAE - Turns the finished render into a picture. It works with four channels, red, green, blue and transparency, which is how this model can make transparent pictures.

 The speed node

Teal, above the graph.

  • Model Attention Backend - Set to comfy kitchen attention, a faster way to do the model's attention maths. The Run Times note has the numbers. On a graphics card that cannot use it, ComfyUI falls back to normal attention by itself.

 The numbers you set

Blue, and numbered. These are the only nodes you have to touch.

  • 1. Load Image - The design you are editing: a poster, a logo, 3D lettering, a flyer. The result keeps its shape.
  • 2. Output Size - How many pixels the result has. Pick a line from the list: 1024 is about 1 megapixel and fast, 2048 is Ming's 2K and slower. Your picture keeps its shape either way.
  • 3. Add a prompt - The one change you want, and what to keep. Put any words you want written in quotes.
  • 4. Seed Random/Fixed? - Fixed repeats the same result, Random rolls a new one each Run.

 The helpers

Purple. They run by themselves.

  • Scale Image to Total Pixels - Works out the exact size at the Output Size you picked: that many pixels, in steps of 32, in your picture's shape. Only that size is used.
  • Get Image Size - Reads that size as a width and a height for the nodes that need it.
  • Resize Crop Pixaroma - Scales your picture to that size and crops the few pixels that do not fit, so nothing is stretched and the result lines up with your picture in the Compare.
  • ModelSamplingFlux - Tunes the model to the size of the result. 1.15 and 0.5 are the settings from ComfyUI's own template.

 The render

Green. These run by themselves.

  • Text Encode Ming Image Edit - Reads your prompt and your picture. It has room for up to 8 pictures; this workflow uses one.
  • ConditioningZeroOut - An empty negative prompt. This model is made for CFG 1, where the negative does nothing, but the KSampler needs one plugged in.
  • Empty Latent Image - The blank canvas for the result, at the size from the helpers.
  • KSampler - The render: 12 steps, lcm, simple, CFG 1. ComfyUI's own template uses a chain of custom sampler nodes with a tuned lcm sampler; the plain KSampler gave results of the same quality and the same layout in 10 test pairs, so the simpler one stays.
  • VAE Decode - Turns the finished render into a picture.

 The result

Dark red, at the end.

  • Image Compare Pixaroma - Your picture and the result, one over the other. Move the mouse across it to slide between them.
  • Preview Image Pixaroma - Shows the result and saves it to your output folder as a PNG.

The dark Run Timer above them shows how long the last Run took.

","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Nodes Info","icon":"node-v5","color":"#3d7cc9"}}

{"version":1,"content":"

SETTINGS

 What this workflow makes

A new style for a design you already have, with Ming Image 0.1 Design: here, a flat vector poster of a fox becomes a clean 3D render with the same layout, colours and headline. In the tests the flat to 3D restyle worked on 4 of 4 seeds, and the headline stayed spelled right.

Load your own flat design (a poster, an icon, a logo, an illustration) and keep the prompt's last sentence, which is what holds the layout and the text in place.

Restyle triedWorked
Flat vector poster to clean 3D render4 of 4
Neon poster to flat vector0 of 4, barely changed

Going from flat to 3D is what Ming does reliably; the other way round, from a busy neon picture to flat vector, it barely changed the picture.

 Writing the prompt

  • Say the one change, then what to keep: the demo says Same layout, same colors, same headline.
  • Put every word you want written in quotes.
  • One change per Run works best. Asked to recolour two things at once, Ming changed only one of them; run it again on the result for the second.
  • A change of style worked from flat to 3D, not the other way round: the neon poster asked to become flat vector barely changed.
  • Leave room for new text. On a photo where a person fills the frame, ask to pull the camera back a little, or a headline can land on the face.
","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Settings","icon":"gear","color":"#2a9d8f"}}

{"version":1,"content":"

RUN TIMES

Every number below was measured on a 24 GB RTX 4090 with this workflow and its own settings, each run on a fresh seed with the models already loaded. A different card gives different numbers, but the shape holds: the cost goes up with the pixels.

 How long a Run takes

Output SizeResultNew picture or promptNew seed only
1024 - about 1 MP1024 x 102410 s5.5 s
1536 - about 2.4 MP1536 x 153618 s14 s
2048 - about 4 MP, 2K2048 x 204835 s30 s

The result sizes are for a square picture like the demo one. Change the picture or the prompt and the text encoder reads them again, which is the first time column. Change only the seed and it reuses what it read, which is the second.

This workflow opens at 1024, the quickest. Go up to 1536 or 2048 for the result you keep.

 Kitchen attention

The teal Model Attention Backend node is set to comfy kitchen attention, a faster way to do the attention maths. On the same seed at Output Size 2048, it took 30 s, against 55 s with the normal pytorch attention. The result was a different variation, not a worse one. In a test that had to keep a portrait exactly as it was, normal attention kept slightly more of it unchanged on 3 of 4 seeds, so switch to pytorch attention when the edit must touch as little as possible. To compare it yourself, switch the node to pytorch attention.

It needs an Nvidia or AMD graphics card. On anything else ComfyUI falls back to normal attention by itself, so the workflow still runs.

 The first Run of the session

The first Run after starting ComfyUI has to load 5.75 GB of image model and 18.2 GB of text encoder. Measured on a 1024 edit: 13 s with the models unloaded first, 10 s once they were loaded. At 1536: 23 s against 18 s.

That was with the model files still in this machine's file cache. The very first load after switching the computer on reads them off the disk for real and will be slower; that case was not measured, so no number is given for it.

 Smaller graphics cards

ComfyUI loads this model in pieces, so it does not have to fit on the card in one go. In a test where ComfyUI was told to use only about 8 GB of this card, an edit went past that, to about 11.5 GB, because reading your picture takes extra working memory; text to image stayed within it. With nothing limiting it, it took about 23 GB of this 24 GB card: ComfyUI uses the room it has.

That test ran on a 4090, so it shows what fits, not how fast a smaller card is. A slower card takes longer, and Output Size 2048 takes three to five times as long as 1024. That is why this workflow opens at 1024.

 System RAM

With the whole card to itself, ComfyUI held 6 to 9 GB of RAM. The smaller the card, the more of the models wait in RAM instead: up to about 22 GB when it was told to use 6 GB of the card. Plan on 32 GB of RAM at the very least. A smaller version of the text encoder (w4a8, 12.8 GB) is in the More versions list; it was not tested here.

","buttonColor":"#f66744","lineColor":"#f66744","backgroundColor":"#2a2a2a","info":{"title":"Run Times","icon":"run-timer","color":"#3f9a4f"}}
